title: Implement Data Privacy and Compliance Controls
intro: Privacy by Design applied to AI (purpose, lawful basis, consent, minimisation and privacy-friendly architecture); the protection techniques that let AI use data safely (masking, tokenisation, pseudonymisation, anonymisation, noise injection and differential privacy); what the GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS require of AI systems, and the wider regulatory map; and the privacy challenges unique to AI, especially unintentional bias and the right to erasure.
objectives: Apply Privacy by Design principles, including purpose limitation, lawful basis, consent and minimisation, to AI systems and architectures
Select data protection techniques for AI pipelines and distinguish pseudonymised from anonymised data
Explain differential privacy, the privacy budget and where noise can be injected
Apply GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS requirements to AI data flows, including Article 22, de-identification and cardholder data scope
Manage AI-specific privacy challenges: memorisation, inference, false personal data, unintentional bias and erasure from models
Apply the mechanics of differential privacy: sensitivity, noise mechanisms, composition, DP-SGD and the questions that test a privacy claim

sections.title: Privacy by Design for AI systems

blocks.title: Privacy built in, not bolted on

scenes.title: Privacy built in, not bolted on
scenes.sub: Privacy by Design principles applied to AI
scenes.say: Privacy is cheapest and most effective when it is designed in from the start. Retrofitting it to a trained model is expensive, and sometimes impossible. | This video covers the Privacy by Design principles and how to apply them to AI systems, from purpose and consent to minimisation and privacy-friendly architecture.

scenes.title: Seven foundational principles

items.d: Prevent privacy harms before they happen
Protected without the user doing anything
Part of the architecture, not an add-on
Positive-sum: privacy and utility together
Protection across the whole lifecycle
Practices open to verification
User-centric choices and controls

scenes.say: Privacy by Design rests on seven foundational principles, first set out by Ann Cavoukian. | Be proactive, not reactive: prevent privacy harms before they happen. | Make privacy the default: people are protected without having to do anything. | Embed privacy into the design and architecture, rather than adding it afterwards. | Aim for full functionality: privacy and usefulness together, not a trade where one side loses. | Provide end-to-end security across the whole data lifecycle. | Keep practices visible and transparent, so they can be verified. | And respect the user, with user-centric defaults, notices and controls. The GDPR turned the idea into law as data protection by design and by default.

scenes.title: Privacy decisions at design time
scenes.say: Applied to AI, Privacy by Design is a sequence of design decisions. Start with a specific, documented purpose. A vague purpose such as improving our services justifies nothing. | Choose a lawful basis for each processing activity, whether consent or another basis, and record why. | Minimise: only the fields, records and retention the purpose genuinely needs. | Choose an architecture that limits exposure. For example, retrieval keeps personal data in a deletable index, rather than baking it into model weights through fine-tuning. | Set protective defaults, such as opting in to training rather than opting out, and short retention of prompts. | And be transparent, with clear notices and controls people can actually use.

scenes.title: Purpose limitation in practice
rows: AI that drafts replies to the same requests
New purpose: assess, inform, possibly consent
scenes.say: Purpose limitation is where many AI projects go wrong. | Imagine data collected to handle customer support requests. | Using it in an AI tool that drafts replies to those same requests is closely related to the original purpose. Using it to train a marketing model that predicts who will buy more is not. | The first is likely compatible, provided people are informed. The second is a new purpose: it needs its own assessment, clear information to customers, and possibly consent.

scenes.title: Privacy-friendly AI architectures

items.d: Keep personal data in deletable indexes, not weights
On-device or on-premises models for sensitive data
Train where the data lives; share only updates
Strip identifiers from prompts and logs

scenes.say: Architecture choices can reduce privacy risk dramatically. | Retrieve rather than memorise: keep personal data in a permission-filtered, deletable index, instead of training it into weights. | Process locally: on-device or on-premises models avoid sending sensitive data to third parties. | Federated learning trains models where the data lives, sharing only model updates, which should themselves be protected with secure aggregation and differential privacy. | And redact before the model: strip identifiers from prompts and logs when the task doesn’t need them.

items: Proactive, default, embedded, positive-sum, secure, visible, user-centric
Specific purpose and lawful basis before any data moves
Minimise fields, records and retention
Prefer architectures that keep personal data out of weights
scenes.say: To recap. | Privacy by Design means being proactive, protective by default, embedded, positive-sum, secure end to end, transparent and user-centric. | Set a specific purpose and lawful basis before any data moves. | Minimise fields, records and retention. | And prefer architectures that keep personal data out of model weights and away from unnecessary parties.

blocks.md:
### Privacy by Design and by default
**Privacy by Design** was articulated by Ann Cavoukian as seven foundational principles: proactive not reactive; privacy as the default setting; privacy embedded into design; full functionality (positive-sum, not zero-sum); end-to-end security across the lifecycle; visibility and transparency; and respect for user privacy. **ISO 31700-1:2023** turned the concept into a consumer-focused standard, and the GDPR made it a legal duty in **Article 25: data protection by design and by default**, requiring appropriate technical and organisational measures (such as pseudonymisation and minimisation) at the time of design, and by default processing only the personal data necessary for each specific purpose.

### Core principles applied to AI
| Principle | What it means for AI | Example controls |
|---|---|---|
| **Purpose limitation** | Collect for specified, explicit, legitimate purposes; don’t reuse incompatibly | Documented purpose per dataset and model; compatibility assessment before reuse; owner approval of new purposes |
| **Lawful basis** | Every processing activity, including training, needs a basis | Basis recorded per activity; legitimate interests assessments; consent records where consent is used |
| **Consent** | Where consent is the basis, it must be freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous and withdrawable | Separate consent for AI training; consent status carried with data; withdrawal honoured downstream |
| **Data minimisation** | Adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary | Feature selection; dropping identifiers; aggregation; sampling; short retention for prompts and logs |
| **Accuracy** | Personal data must be accurate and kept up to date | Correcting training data and indexes; controls on model outputs about individuals |
| **Storage limitation** | Keep no longer than necessary | Retention schedules for datasets, prompts, logs and models |
| **Integrity and confidentiality** | Appropriate security | Encryption, access control, isolation, monitoring |

### Privacy-friendly design patterns
- **Retrieval over fine-tuning for personal data:** data in an index can be access-controlled, corrected and deleted; data in weights is hard to remove.
- **Edge and on-premises inference** for highly sensitive data.
- **Federated learning:** models are trained across devices or organisations without centralising raw data. Updates can still leak information, so combine with **secure aggregation** and **differential privacy**.
- **Redaction and pseudonymisation** of prompts, logs and training data where identities aren’t needed.
- **Privacy-preserving computation:** secure multi-party computation, homomorphic encryption and confidential computing (Module 2.5) for collaborative or outsourced processing.
- **Protective defaults:** opt-in for training use, minimal retention, conversation history off by default for sensitive tools, and clear controls.

### Embedding privacy in the AI lifecycle
Privacy requirements should appear at each lifecycle gate: a privacy review at design (purpose, basis, data inventory), an SDIA and DPIA before data is used, privacy testing before deployment (leakage and memorisation tests, output checks), and monitoring and periodic review in operation. The data protection officer should be consulted on high-risk processing, and their advice recorded.

blocks.title: Match the control to the principle
pairs: Training on aggregated counts instead of individual records
Keeping customer support data out of a marketing model
Conversation history switched off by default in a medical assistant
Correcting false information about a person in a retrieval index

blocks.title: Design time beats run time
blocks.md: When an exam option adds privacy **at design time** (purpose definition, minimisation, architecture that keeps data out of weights, protective defaults) and another adds it **after deployment** (filtering outputs, apologising for breaches), the design-time control is usually the better answer. That is the essence of Privacy by Design.

q.q: A team wants its assistant to answer questions about individual customers’ accounts. Which design BEST follows Privacy by Design?
o: Fine-tune the model on all customer records, then filter answers so each user sees only their own account
Retrieve only the requesting customer’s records at query time, through permission checks, with minimal logging
Load the whole customer database into the system prompt, encrypted at rest, and instruct the model to be discreet
Copy every account into a shared vector index and have staff review a sample of answers each week
q.why: Query-time retrieval with access checks minimises exposure, keeps data deletable and correctable, and limits processing to what each request needs. Fine-tuning would bake personal data into weights.

blocks.title: Protect the data, keep the value

scenes.title: Protect the data, keep the value
scenes.sub: Masking, tokenisation, pseudonymisation, anonymisation, noise and differential privacy
scenes.say: AI teams want rich, realistic data. Privacy teams want as little identifiable data as possible. Protection techniques let you have much of both. | This video compares the main techniques, what each one protects against, and where each fits in an AI pipeline.

scenes.title: Eight techniques to know

items.d: Hide characters or values, e.g. ****1234
Swap values for tokens; originals in a vault
Replace identifiers; re-identifiable with a key
Coarsen values: age 37 becomes 35–39
Remove fields, values or records
No longer relates to an identifiable person
Random perturbation of values or results
Calibrated noise with a provable limit

scenes.say: There are eight techniques to know. | Masking hides part of a value, such as all but the last four digits of a card number. | Tokenisation swaps a value for a meaningless token, and keeps the original in a secured vault. | Pseudonymisation replaces identifiers with pseudonyms, such as keyed hashes. Whoever holds the key can re-identify people, so it is still personal data. | Generalisation coarsens values, such as turning an exact age into a five-year band. | Suppression and redaction remove fields, values or whole records. | Anonymisation is an end state rather than a single technique: data that can no longer identify anyone, by any means reasonably likely to be used. | Noise injection adds random perturbation to values or results. | And differential privacy calibrates that noise mathematically, giving a provable limit on what anyone can learn about one person.

scenes.title: How tokenisation works
scenes.say: Here is tokenisation for payments. A card number arrives at the payment edge. | A tokenisation service replaces it with a random token that has no mathematical link to the card number. | The mapping lives only in a heavily protected vault, often backed by a hardware security module. | Downstream systems, including AI models, analytics and logs, see only tokens. If they leak, the tokens are worthless, and systems that can’t reach the vault may fall out of PCI DSS scope. | Only a few authorised payment systems can detokenise. Consistent tokens, where the same card always gets the same token, keep the data useful for joining and modelling.

scenes.title: Pseudonymised or anonymised?
rows: Possible with a key or extra data
Keyed hashes, tokens, coded study IDs
High bar: models rarely qualify by default
scenes.say: The difference between pseudonymised and anonymised data is one of the most tested ideas in privacy. | Pseudonymised data can be re-identified with a key or extra information. Anonymised data can’t be re-identified by anyone, using means reasonably likely to be used. And removing names isn’t enough: postcode, birth date and sex together single out most people. | So pseudonymised data is still personal data under the GDPR, while truly anonymised data falls outside it. The EU Court of Justice has added that pseudonymised data may not be personal data for a recipient with no reasonable means of re-identifying it. | Pseudonymisation includes keyed hashes, consistent tokens and coded study identifiers. Anonymisation might be robust aggregate statistics, or synthetic data tested for leakage. | The AI implication: pseudonymisation reduces risk but keeps your obligations, and a model trained on personal data isn’t automatically anonymous. That has to be demonstrated.

scenes.title: The privacy budget trade-off
scenes.yLabel: Illustrative results at each privacy budget (ε)

notes.d: The privacy budget. Smaller ε means more noise and stronger privacy.
Accuracy falls, hardest for small groups and rare cases.
Membership inference falls towards a coin toss (50%).
Agree ε with the data owner and privacy team; track the total spent.

scenes.say: Differential privacy has one key dial: epsilon, the privacy budget. A smaller epsilon means more noise and a stronger guarantee: the output barely changes whether or not any one person is included. | The cost is utility. In this illustrative example, accuracy drops as epsilon shrinks, hardest for small groups and rare cases. | The benefit is privacy. Membership inference, guessing whether someone was in the training data, falls towards a coin toss. | So choosing epsilon is a policy decision. Agree it with the data owner and the privacy team, and track the total budget spent, because every release uses some of it.

scenes.title: Where noise can be injected

nodes.label: Collection
nodes.sub: local DP: noise on the device

scenes.say: Noise can be injected at three points. At collection, local differential privacy adds noise on the user’s own device, so even the collector never sees true values. | During training, DP-SGD clips each example’s influence on the model and adds calibrated noise, limiting how much it can memorise any single record. | At release, noise is added to published statistics, or used to generate differentially private synthetic data. | And a privacy accountant tracks the cumulative budget, because privacy loss adds up across every release.

items: Masking and tokenisation protect values; tokens need a secured vault
Pseudonymised data is still personal data
Anonymisation is an outcome to prove, not a step to assume
Differential privacy trades accuracy for a provable limit, set by ε
scenes.say: To recap. | Masking and tokenisation protect specific values, and tokenisation depends on a well-protected vault. | Pseudonymised data is still personal data. | Anonymisation is an outcome to demonstrate, not a step to assume. | And differential privacy trades some accuracy for a provable privacy limit, set by epsilon.

blocks.md:
### Choosing a protection technique
| Technique | How it works | Reversible? | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Masking** | Hides characters or substitutes fake values. *Static* masking makes a masked copy; *dynamic* masking hides values at display time | Static copy: no. Dynamic: original intact | Dynamic masking doesn’t protect the stored data |
| **Tokenisation** | Replaces values with tokens; the mapping sits in a secure vault | Yes, by authorised systems via the vault | The vault becomes a crown jewel; consistent tokens are pseudonyms |
| **Encryption** (including format-preserving) | Transforms data with a key | Yes, with the key | Key management; encrypted personal data is still personal data |
| **Hashing** | One-way function; use a keyed hash (HMAC) | Not directly | Unkeyed hashes of predictable values, such as phone or card numbers, can be reversed by trying every value |
| **Pseudonymisation** | Replaces identifiers; re-identification information kept separately and protected | Yes, for the key holder | Still personal data (GDPR Article 4(5)) |
| **Generalisation and suppression** | Coarsens values; removes rare combinations and outliers | No | Utility loss; weak alone against linkage |
| **Redaction** | Removes identifiers from text, images and audio | No | Misses unusual formats and contextual clues |
| **Noise injection** | Adds random perturbation to values or outputs | No | No guarantee unless calibrated; repeated queries can average it out |
| **Differential privacy** | Noise calibrated to a privacy budget (ε) | No | Utility loss, especially for small groups |

### Anonymisation and pseudonymisation in law
Under the GDPR, anonymous information is outside scope (Recital 26), judged against *all the means reasonably likely to be used*, considering cost, time and technology. Pseudonymised data remains personal data. In **EDPS v SRB** (C-413/23 P, September 2025) the Court of Justice held that pseudonymised data isn’t necessarily personal data *for a recipient* with no reasonable means of re-identification, though the original controller’s duties are judged from its own perspective. The Commission’s Digital Omnibus proposed writing this into the GDPR; as of October 2026 those amendments had not been adopted.

For AI models, the EDPB’s **Opinion 28/2024** says a model trained on personal data is anonymous only if the likelihood of extracting personal data from it, directly or through queries, is insignificant, and this must be demonstrated and documented. The UK ICO’s **motivated intruder test** asks whether a competent person without specialist skills, but with access to public resources, could re-identify people.

### Why de-identification fails
Latanya Sweeney found that zip code, date of birth and sex uniquely identified about 87% of Americans, and researchers re-identified Netflix Prize subscribers by linking their movie ratings with public reviews. Such **quasi-identifiers** enable **linkage**. Formal models reduce the risk: **k-anonymity** (each record matches at least k−1 others on its quasi-identifiers), **l-diversity** (each group holds several well-represented sensitive values) and **t-closeness** (each group’s sensitive values are distributed like the whole dataset’s). They don’t protect against arbitrary background knowledge; differential privacy does.

### Differential privacy in brief
A mechanism is **ε-differentially private** if its output is almost equally likely whether or not any one person’s data is included. Key ideas:
- **Sensitivity**, how much one person can change a result, sets how much noise is needed.
- **Composition:** privacy loss adds up across releases, so a **privacy accountant** tracks the budget.
- **Post-processing:** anything computed from a differentially private output stays differentially private.
- **Local vs central:** local DP adds noise before collection; central DP adds noise to results from a trusted curator, with better accuracy.
- **DP-SGD** clips per-example gradients and adds noise during training, limiting memorisation and membership inference.
- **Unit of privacy:** decide whether you protect a record or a person, who may have many records.

NIST SP 800-226 (2025) gives guidance on evaluating differential privacy guarantees.

### Across an AI pipeline
- **Training data:** minimise, pseudonymise identifiers, redact free text, de-duplicate, and use DP-SGD for highly sensitive data.
- **Retrieval corpora:** redact or tokenise before indexing, and filter retrieval by permission.
- **Prompts and outputs:** redact or tokenise personal data before it reaches an external model (Module 3.4 covers DLP).
- **Logs:** mask by default, keep retention short and restrict access to raw logs.
- **Non-production:** use masked or synthetic data only.
- **Reporting:** aggregate, suppress small counts or apply differential privacy.

blocks.title: Technique flashcards
cards: Tokens replace sensitive values; the mapping lives only in a secured vault. Systems that never touch the vault can fall out of scope.
A hash computed with a secret key. Without the key, predictable inputs such as phone numbers can’t be recovered by trying every value.
Every record shares its quasi-identifier values with at least k−1 others, so no one can be singled out on those attributes alone.
The parameter bounding how much a differentially private output can reveal about one person. Spending accumulates across releases.
Training that clips each example’s gradient and adds calibrated noise, limiting memorisation and membership inference at some cost to accuracy.

blocks.title: Classic traps
blocks.md:
- **Hashing or tokenising an identifier is pseudonymisation, not anonymisation.** The data remains personal data.
- **Removing names is not anonymisation.** Quasi-identifiers and linkage can re-identify people.
- **Encryption protects confidentiality, not identifiability.** Encrypted personal data is still personal data.
- When an option offers a **provable** limit on what can be learned about an individual, it is pointing at **differential privacy**.

q.q: A data science team wants to train a fraud model on transaction data and must link each customer’s transactions over time, without exposing real account numbers to the team. Which technique BEST fits?
o: Delete the account number column and rely on transaction timestamps to group each customer’s activity
Replace account numbers with consistent tokens or keyed-hash pseudonyms, with the key held by another team
Encrypt the account number column and give the team the key, so that joins across tables still work
Keep the real account numbers but add calibrated noise to every amount, so no individual can be identified
q.why: Consistent pseudonyms let records be linked without revealing real identifiers, and separating the key keeps re-identification under control. Deleting the column breaks linkage, sharing the key exposes the data, and noise on amounts doesn’t protect identifiers. The result is still personal data and must be governed as such.

sections.title: Global privacy regulations: GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS

scenes.title: Three rulebooks, one AI system
scenes.sub: What the GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS require of AI
scenes.say: One AI assistant can fall under several privacy regimes at once: European data protection law, US health privacy rules, and the card industry’s security standard. | This video covers what the GDPR, HIPAA and PCI DSS require of AI systems.

scenes.title: How the three regimes differ
rows: Personal data of people in the EU
Anyone storing, processing or sending card data
scenes.say: Start with how the three differ. | The GDPR is an EU regulation with global reach. HIPAA is a US federal law. PCI DSS isn’t a law at all: it’s an industry standard, enforced through contracts. | The GDPR protects personal data about people in the EU. HIPAA protects protected health information. PCI DSS protects cardholder data, such as the card number, and sensitive authentication data, such as the security code. | The GDPR applies to controllers and processors in the EU, and to those elsewhere that target or monitor people in the EU. HIPAA covers health plans, clearinghouses, most healthcare providers, and their business associates. PCI DSS covers anyone who stores, processes or transmits card data. | Data protection authorities can fine up to four percent of worldwide annual turnover. The HHS Office for Civil Rights enforces HIPAA. And card brands enforce PCI DSS through acquiring banks, with fines, higher fees or loss of the ability to take cards.

scenes.title: The GDPR meets AI

items.d: Training and deployment are separate purposes
Limits on solely automated significant decisions
Required where high risk is likely
Access, rectification, erasure, objection
Adequacy, SCCs and transfer assessments
72 hours to the supervisory authority

scenes.say: The GDPR touches AI in six main ways. | Each purpose needs a lawful basis. Training and deployment are usually separate purposes, and relying on legitimate interests needs a documented balancing test. | Article 22 restricts solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects. | A data protection impact assessment is required where high risk is likely, which covers most AI that profiles people or uses sensitive data at scale. | Rights of access, rectification, erasure and objection apply, and are hard to honour once data is inside a model. | Sending personal data to a model hosted outside the European Economic Area is a transfer, needing an adequacy decision, standard contractual clauses or another mechanism. | And personal data breaches must be reported to the supervisory authority within seventy-two hours of becoming aware, unless unlikely to result in risk.

scenes.title: The Article 22 test
scenes.say: Article 22 works like a test. First: is the decision solely automated? A human who just rubber-stamps the model’s output doesn’t count as meaningful involvement. | Second: does it have legal or similarly significant effects, such as refusing credit or rejecting a job application? | If both are true, the decision is allowed only when it is necessary for a contract, authorised by law, or based on explicit consent. | If no exception applies, redesign the process, typically with genuine human review. | Where an exception does apply, people must be able to obtain human intervention, express their view and contest the decision, and they are entitled to meaningful information about the logic involved.

scenes.title: HIPAA meets AI

items.d: Training data, prompts, logs and outputs
Treatment, payment, operations; else authorisation
Only the PHI the purpose needs
Required before an AI vendor handles PHI
Administrative, physical, technical safeguards
Safe Harbor or Expert Determination

scenes.say: HIPAA applies wherever protected health information flows through an AI system. | That includes training data, prompts, retrieved records, logs and outputs, such as drafted clinical notes. | PHI can be used for treatment, payment and healthcare operations. Most other uses, such as training a commercial product, need patient authorisation or de-identified data. | The minimum necessary standard argues against sending whole records to a model when a few fields will do. | An AI vendor that handles PHI on a covered entity’s behalf is a business associate, and needs a business associate agreement before any PHI flows. | The Security Rule requires administrative, physical and technical safeguards, starting with a risk analysis that includes the AI system. | And properly de-identified data is no longer PHI. Safe Harbor removes eighteen types of identifier; Expert Determination relies on a qualified expert finding the re-identification risk very small.

scenes.title: How a chatbot pulls in PCI DSS scope

nodes.label: Hosted payment page
nodes.sub: card data never enters the chat

nodes.label: Detect and redact
nodes.sub: before the model and the logs

scenes.say: Now PCI DSS. Imagine a customer types their card number into a support chat. | The assistant passes it to a model API, and transcripts and logs store it. All of these systems, and the vendors behind them, are now in PCI DSS scope. | The best fix is design: hand payments off to a PCI-compliant hosted payment page, so card data never enters the chat. | As a backstop, detect and redact card numbers before they reach the model or the logs, and never retain the security code after authorisation.

scenes.title: PCI DSS v4.0.1 rules that bite in AI

items.d: AI tools that touch card data are in scope
Not in transcripts, recordings or logs
BIN and last four digits at most
Tokens, truncation, keyed hashes, strong crypto
Written agreements and monitoring

scenes.say: Five PCI DSS requirements bite hardest in AI. | Confirm scope at least every twelve months. Any AI tool that touches card data, or can affect its security, is in scope. | Never store sensitive authentication data, such as the security code, after authorisation, even encrypted. That includes transcripts, recordings and logs. | Mask card numbers on display, showing at most the bank identification number and the last four digits. | Render stored card numbers unreadable, using tokens, truncation, keyed hashes or strong encryption. | And treat AI vendors that handle card data as third-party service providers, with written agreements and ongoing monitoring.

items: GDPR: lawful basis, Article 22, DPIAs, rights, transfers, 72-hour breach reports
HIPAA: permitted uses, minimum necessary, BAAs, de-identification
PCI DSS: keep card data out of AI; tokenise, mask, never store SAD
Map every AI data flow to every regime that applies
scenes.say: To recap. | The GDPR brings lawful basis, Article 22, impact assessments, rights, transfer rules and seventy-two-hour breach reporting. | HIPAA brings permitted uses, minimum necessary, business associate agreements and two de-identification routes. | PCI DSS is best met by keeping card data out of AI systems altogether. | And because one AI system can fall under all three, map every data flow to every regime that applies.

blocks.md:
### GDPR essentials for AI
| Element | Key provisions | How it applies to AI |
|---|---|---|
| **Principles** | Article 5 | Apply equally to training, retrieval, prompts, logs and outputs |
| **Lawful basis** | Article 6; Article 9 for special category data | Training often relies on legitimate interests: purpose, necessity and balancing tests, with mitigations (EDPB Opinion 28/2024) |
| **Transparency** | Articles 12–14 | Tell people about AI use, including training and automated decisions; Article 14 covers indirectly collected data, such as scraped data |
| **Rights** | Articles 15–22 | Honour across datasets, indexes, logs and, where feasible, models |
| **Accountability** | Articles 25, 28, 30, 32, 35 and 37 | AI appears in records of processing, DPIAs, security measures and processor contracts |
| **Breaches** | Articles 33–34 | Tell the authority within 72 hours unless unlikely to result in risk; tell individuals without undue delay when risk is high |
| **Transfers** | Chapter V | Adequacy decisions (including the EU–US Data Privacy Framework for certified organisations), standard contractual clauses, binding corporate rules |
| **Penalties** | Article 83 | Up to €20 million or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher |

**Article 22.** People have the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing, including profiling, with legal or similarly significant effects, unless the decision is necessary for a contract, authorised by law, or based on explicit consent. Even then, safeguards apply: human intervention, the chance to express a view, and the right to contest. Articles 13–15 require **meaningful information about the logic involved**. In **SCHUFA** (C-634/21, 2023) the Court of Justice treated a credit score as an automated decision where it played a determining role in a lender’s decision. In **Dun & Bradstreet Austria** (C-203/22, 2025) it held that people are entitled to an explanation of the procedure and principles actually applied, and that trade secrets can’t justify a blanket refusal. The UK’s **Data (Use and Access) Act 2025** relaxes some UK automated decision-making limits where special category data isn’t involved, while keeping safeguards.

**Reform watch.** The Commission’s November 2025 **Digital Omnibus** proposed GDPR changes, including a legitimate-interest route for AI development. As of October 2026 they had not been adopted (the Council agreed its negotiating position that month), so the current GDPR applies. The separate AI Act changes were adopted as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

### HIPAA essentials for AI
- **Who:** covered entities (health plans, healthcare clearinghouses, and providers that conduct standard electronic transactions) and their business associates, including subcontractors. Many consumer health apps fall outside HIPAA, though other rules, such as the FTC’s Health Breach Notification Rule, may apply.
- **Privacy Rule:** uses for treatment, payment and healthcare operations; patient authorisation for most other purposes; the minimum necessary standard; rights of access and amendment.
- **Security Rule:** administrative, physical and technical safeguards, some *required* and some *addressable*. A proposed update published in January 2025 would make encryption and MFA mandatory; at the time of writing it had not been finalised.
- **Breach Notification Rule:** notify individuals within 60 days of discovering a breach of unsecured PHI, and notify HHS; breaches affecting more than 500 residents of a state or jurisdiction also require media notice. PHI encrypted in line with HHS guidance is “secured”.
- **De-identification:** **Safe Harbor** removes 18 identifiers (including names, geographic units smaller than a state, all date elements except the year, contact details, record and device numbers, IP addresses, biometrics and full-face photographs), with no actual knowledge that the rest could identify someone. **Expert Determination** relies on a qualified expert’s documented statistical analysis. A **limited data set** keeps some dates and locations under a data use agreement.
- **AI implications:** confirm the permitted purpose before training on PHI; use BAAs that restrict a vendor’s own use of PHI, such as training its general models; apply minimum necessary to prompts and retrieval; and test de-identified training data for memorisation.

### PCI DSS essentials for AI
- **Version:** PCI DSS v4.0.1 (June 2024) is current; its future-dated requirements became mandatory on 31 March 2025.
- **Account data:** cardholder data (primary account number (PAN), cardholder name, expiry date, service code) plus **sensitive authentication data** (full track data, card verification codes, PINs).
- **Scope:** systems that store, process or transmit account data, or that connect to or could affect them. Scope is confirmed at least every 12 months and after significant change (Requirement 12.5.2).
- **Requirement 3:** never retain SAD after authorisation; mask PAN when displayed; render stored PAN unreadable (keyed hashes of the full PAN, truncation, tokens or strong cryptography with key management).
- **Also relevant:** strong cryptography in transit (Requirement 4), least privilege and MFA (Requirements 7–8), logging (Requirement 10) and service provider management (Requirement 12.8).
- **AI guidance:** the PCI SSC’s *AI Principles: Securing the Use of AI in Payment Environments* (September 2025) say AI systems must comply with applicable PCI requirements, and stress limiting the sensitive data AI can reach, protecting credentials, logging AI activity and using tokens where full card numbers aren’t needed.
- **AI implications:** use hosted payment pages, or pause-and-resume and keypad entry on calls; redact before models and logs; treat AI vendors as service providers; never train models on card data.

### The wider map
| Jurisdiction | Main laws | AI-relevant points |
|---|---|---|
| **UK** | UK GDPR, Data Protection Act 2018, Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 | Close to the GDPR; ICO guidance on AI and data protection |
| **EU** | GDPR alongside the AI Act | Data governance for high-risk AI (Article 10); bias testing with special category data (see Section 4) |
| **US: California** | CCPA as amended by the CPRA | Rights to know, delete, correct and opt out; rules on automated decision-making technology, risk assessments and cybersecurity audits, phasing in from 2026 |
| **US: federal and other states** | Sector laws (HIPAA, GLBA, COPPA), state privacy laws, the FTC Act | The FTC has ordered companies to delete models built on improperly obtained data (“algorithmic disgorgement”) |
| **Brazil, China, India** | LGPD; PIPL; Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 | Review of automated decisions (LGPD); transparency, refusal rights and transfer assessments (PIPL); consent-centred duties phasing in (DPDP) |

blocks.title: Which rule is this?
pairs: Notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours
Sign an agreement before an AI vendor handles PHI
Never keep the card security code after authorisation
Right not to be subject to solely automated significant decisions
Confirm scope at least every 12 months

blocks.title: The AI scribe
blocks.md: A private hospital group operating in Germany and the United States plans an AI scribe. It records consultations, drafts clinical notes using a cloud-hosted model in the US, and lets patients settle bills by reading out their card details during the call.

q.q: Which approach BEST addresses the group’s privacy obligations?
o: Rely on the vendor’s ISO 27001 certification and standard terms, since the vendor processes the data and carries compliance responsibility for it
DPIA and HIPAA risk analysis; a BAA and GDPR processor terms with transfer safeguards; minimised model input; card payments taken outside the recording
Encrypt recordings and notes end to end, host the model in the EU for all patients, and treat all three regimes as satisfied by that design
Sign a BAA covering all patients, because HIPAA’s safeguards are stricter than the GDPR’s and so satisfy both regimes at once
q.why: All three regimes apply: the GDPR for German patients (including the transfer to the US), HIPAA for US PHI and the vendor relationship, and PCI DSS for card data captured in calls. Accountability stays with the hospital group, encryption or hosting location alone doesn’t meet any regime, and HIPAA compliance doesn’t satisfy the GDPR.

blocks.title: Know what each regime is
blocks.md:
- **PCI DSS is a contractual industry standard**, not a law. Non-compliance leads to fines and sanctions through card brands and acquirers.
- **HIPAA applies to covered entities and business associates**, not to all health data everywhere.
- **The GDPR follows the person**, not the server: processing EU residents’ data with a model hosted elsewhere still falls within scope.
- The best answers **map data flows to every applicable regime** rather than picking one.

q.q: A US health insurer wants a cloud LLM provider to summarise claims files containing PHI. What must be in place BEFORE any PHI is sent?
o: Written authorisation from every affected member, collected before each of their claims files is summarised
A business associate agreement, with the flow covered by the risk analysis and limited to the minimum necessary
Confirmation that the provider holds SOC 2 certification and encrypts all customer data at rest and in transit
Nothing further, because summarising claims is a payment activity that HIPAA permits without any agreement
q.why: A vendor that receives or processes PHI on a covered entity’s behalf is a business associate and needs a BAA first. The risk analysis and minimum necessary standard also apply. Claims processing falls within payment and healthcare operations, so individual authorisation isn’t normally required, but the vendor relationship still needs a BAA. Certifications are useful evidence, not a substitute.

sections.title: AI-specific privacy challenges: bias and erasure

scenes.title: Where privacy meets machine learning
scenes.sub: Memorisation, inference, false facts, unintentional bias and the right to erasure
scenes.say: Traditional privacy controls assume data sits in rows you can find, correct and delete. Machine learning breaks that assumption. | This video covers the privacy challenges specific to AI, focusing on unintentional bias and the right to erasure.

scenes.title: Six AI-specific privacy challenges

items.d: Models can reproduce training data
Was this person in the training set?
Sensitive traits deduced from ordinary data
Hallucinated personal data
Unequal outcomes nobody intended
Hard to honour inside model weights

scenes.say: Six challenges stand out. | Memorisation: models can reproduce fragments of their training data, including personal details. | Membership inference: testing whether a person’s record was in the training data, which can itself be sensitive, for example in a dataset of patients. | Attribute inference: deducing traits such as health conditions from ordinary data. Inferences about people are personal data. | False facts: a model states untrue things about a real person, breaching the accuracy principle. | Unintentional bias: unequal outcomes for groups of people that nobody intended. | And rights, especially erasure, are hard to honour once data is inside model weights.

scenes.title: Removing the attribute didn’t remove the gap

notes.d: The model approves Group B far less often.
Postcode, spending and job history stand in for the attribute.
Measuring the gap needs the sensitive attribute, which minimisation restricts.
Safeguarded testing and mitigation narrow the gap.

scenes.say: Unintentional bias often has a privacy twist. In this illustrative lending model, Group B is approved far less often than Group A. | The obvious fix is to remove the protected attribute, but the gap barely moves, because postcode, spending and job history act as proxies. Fairness through unawareness fails. | To measure bias you need to know who is in each group, which collides with minimisation and the extra protection for special category data. | With safeguarded use of that data for testing and mitigation, the gap narrows. The tension is managed, not avoided.

scenes.title: Resolving the fairness–privacy tension
scenes.say: Here is how to resolve that tension. Start from a genuine need: you can’t detect bias against a group without knowing who is in it. | Try synthetic, anonymised or aggregate data first. | If real sensitive data is strictly necessary, establish a legal basis, such as a GDPR Article 9 condition. The EU AI Act permits this for bias detection in high-risk systems, and the twenty twenty-six Digital Omnibus extended it to other AI systems and models, under strict safeguards. | Process the data in a segregated, access-controlled environment, with no reuse for other purposes. | Measure outcomes by group, mitigate, and record what you changed. | Then delete the sensitive data and document the whole process.

scenes.title: Erasure options for a trained model
scenes.say: When someone asks for erasure and their data trained a model, there are three options. | Retrain without their data; use machine unlearning to remove its influence; or suppress outputs about them. | Retraining gives the highest assurance, because the new model never saw the data. Unlearning varies and is hard to verify. Suppression is lowest, because the data stays in the weights. | Costs run the other way, so many organisations suppress straight away, then remove the data at the next scheduled retraining.

scenes.title: Designing for unlearning: SISA training

steps.show: s1 s2 s3 data-s1 data-s2 data-s3

note.text: Erasing a record retrains only the shard that held it.

scenes.say: Unlearning is far easier if you design for it. SISA training stands for sharded, isolated, sliced and aggregated. | The data is split into shards, and each shard trains its own sub-model in isolation. | At prediction time, the sub-models’ outputs are combined. | To erase a record, only its shard is retrained. That is far cheaper than retraining everything, and the new sub-model has never seen the data. The trade-off is some loss of accuracy.

scenes.title: False facts about a real person

msgs.t: What can you tell me about [a named local doctor]?
They were struck off the medical register in 2021 after a misconduct investigation.
Untrue. The model blended details of two different people with similar names.

notes.d: False output about a person breaches the accuracy principle, and they can demand correction.

scenes.say: A user asks a general-purpose assistant about a named local doctor. | It claims, confidently, that the doctor was struck off for misconduct. | That’s false: the model blended two different people. Personal data must be accurate, and people can demand rectification. The provider can’t simply edit the weights, so it corrects grounding sources, filters outputs about the person, and fixes the model over time.

items: Memorisation and inference make models a privacy risk in themselves
Removing protected attributes doesn’t remove bias: proxies remain
Bias testing may need sensitive data: strictly necessary, safeguarded, deleted
Erasure: retrain, unlearn or suppress, by documented policy
scenes.say: To recap. | Memorisation and inference make a model a privacy risk in itself, not just its data. | Removing protected attributes doesn’t remove bias, because proxies remain. | Bias testing may need sensitive data: used only when strictly necessary, safeguarded, then deleted. | And erasure from models means retraining, unlearning or suppression, chosen by a documented policy.

blocks.md:
### Privacy risks specific to AI
| Risk | What happens | Controls |
|---|---|---|
| **Memorisation** | Models reproduce training data, especially duplicated or rare records | De-duplication; removing personal data before training; DP-SGD; output filtering; extraction testing (Module 3.3) |
| **Membership inference** | Someone determines whether a person’s data was in the training set | Differential privacy; returning labels rather than confidence scores; rate limiting |
| **Model inversion and attribute inference** | Reconstructing features of training data, or inferring sensitive traits | Limit output detail; access control; treat inferences as personal data |
| **Hallucinated personal data** | False statements about real people | Grounding; declining questions about private individuals; output filters; a rectification process |
| **Children’s data** | Extra protection under the GDPR (Article 8), the UK Age Appropriate Design Code and COPPA | Age assurance; high-privacy defaults |

If a model can’t be shown to be anonymous (EDPB Opinion 28/2024), data protection obligations, including rights, extend to it. Complaints are already testing this: in 2025 the privacy group noyb complained to Norway’s data protection authority after a chatbot falsely described a man as having murdered his children, arguing that inaccurate output breaches the GDPR’s accuracy principle.

### Unintentional bias
Bias arises without intent from **historical bias** in data, **representation bias** (under-sampled groups), **measurement bias** (labels or proxies that mean different things for different groups) and **drift** after deployment (Module 2.2 covers fairness metrics). In a well-known case, a US healthcare algorithm used healthcare *costs* as a proxy for health *need*; because less had historically been spent on Black patients with the same needs, it under-identified them for extra care (Obermeyer and colleagues, 2019).

Why it is a privacy issue as well as a fairness one:
- The GDPR’s **fairness** principle and Recital 71 call for measures against discriminatory profiling, and DPIAs must assess discrimination risk.
- **Proxies**, such as postcode, first name or purchase history, defeat “fairness through unawareness”.
- **Privacy techniques can worsen fairness**: differential privacy and aggressive minimisation can reduce accuracy most for small groups, so re-test fairness after applying them.
- **Measuring bias needs sensitive data.** The AI Act lets providers of high-risk systems process special category data where strictly necessary for bias detection and correction (Article 10(5)). The 2026 Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) added **Article 4a**, extending this to other AI systems and models, provided synthetic or anonymised data can’t do the job, reuse is technically limited, security is state of the art, and the data is deleted once the bias is corrected. It permits bias testing; it doesn’t require it.

### The right to erasure
GDPR **Article 17** applies where, for example, data is no longer needed, consent is withdrawn, the person successfully objects, or processing is unlawful. Exceptions include legal obligations, public health, some archiving and research, and legal claims. Controllers must respond within one month (extendable by two further months for complex requests) and tell recipients (Article 19).

The person’s data may sit in source systems, training and evaluation sets, retrieval indexes, prompts, logs, backups, model weights and vendor copies; **lineage** finds it (Module 3.1). For models:
- **Retraining** without the data is exact but costly, so it is often done at the next scheduled retrain.
- **SISA training** retrains only the affected shard: exact and cheaper, with some accuracy cost.
- **Approximate unlearning** is cheaper again, but test afterwards that the model can no longer reproduce the data.
- **Output suppression** is a quick interim measure; the data stays in the weights.

Regulators haven’t settled exactly what erasure requires for model weights, so document your reasoning for each model: whether it can be shown to be anonymous, the risk to the person, the feasibility and cost of each option, and the timeline for removal.

### Rights playbooks and design
- **Access:** search datasets, indexes, prompts and logs, and explain how the data was used, including in decisions.
- **Rectification:** fix sources and indexes, and filter outputs known to be false.
- **Objection:** where you rely on legitimate interests, exclude objectors from future training and honour opt-outs.
- **Automated decisions:** human review, a way to contest, and a meaningful explanation.
- **Design:** keep personal data out of weights where possible, minimise and de-duplicate training data, keep a deletion queue that feeds retraining, consider SISA where erasure requests are expected, and record which model version made each decision (Module 3.5).

blocks.title: The erasure request
blocks.md: A former customer asks a retailer to erase their personal data. Eight months ago, the retailer fine-tuned its recommendation model on purchase histories that included this customer’s. The next scheduled retraining is in two months. The customer’s support tickets also sit in a retrieval index used by the support assistant.

o: Explain that data absorbed into model weights can’t be erased, so only the account record will be deleted
Clean sources, datasets and the index now; suppress outputs if needed; remove it at the next retraining; confirm what was done
Retrain the recommendation model from scratch tonight without their data, then confirm full and final erasure to the customer by email
Delete the account and purchase records but keep the support tickets, because the index holds only derived embeddings
q.why: Erasure must reach every store that lineage identifies. The index and datasets can be cleaned at once; for the model, interim suppression plus removal at the next retraining is proportionate if documented and completed within a defined timeframe. Retraining tonight ignores the index, refusing fails the request, and embeddings derived from personal data are still personal data.

blocks.title: Bias and erasure: answer patterns
blocks.md:
- If an option says **remove the protected attribute to eliminate bias**, it is usually a distractor: proxies remain. Better answers **measure outcomes by group** and mitigate.
- Using sensitive data for bias testing is acceptable when **strictly necessary and safeguarded**, then deleted.
- For erasure from models, the strongest answers are **proportionate and documented**: clean every store now, suppress if needed, and retrain or unlearn on a defined timeline.

q.q: A bank removes ethnicity from its credit model’s inputs, yet approval rates still differ sharply between ethnic groups. What is the MOST likely explanation?
o: The model retains the ethnicity field from earlier training runs and still reads it directly
Other features act as proxies for ethnicity, so the model learns the same pattern indirectly
Approval rates for large groups vary by chance, so the gap is statistical noise to be ignored
Removing an input has no effect until the model is redeployed and its thresholds recalibrated
q.why: Features such as postcode, income patterns or employment history can correlate with ethnicity. “Fairness through unawareness” doesn’t remove bias; outcomes must be measured by group and mitigated.

sections.title: Deep dive: differential privacy in practice

scenes.title: Differential privacy, by the numbers
scenes.sub: Mechanisms, budgets, DP-SGD and how to read a claim
scenes.say: Section two introduced differential privacy and its budget, epsilon. This deep dive shows how the guarantee is actually delivered: the mechanisms that add noise, how budgets add up, and how training itself can be made private. | It ends with the questions to ask when a supplier says its product is differentially private.

scenes.title: One private count, step by step
scenes.say: Start with a simple question for a patient dataset: how many patients have condition X? The true answer is one hundred and twenty. | First, find the sensitivity: the most that one person can change the answer. Adding or removing one patient changes a count by at most one. | The Laplace mechanism adds random noise, with a scale of sensitivity divided by epsilon. With an epsilon of a half, the scale is two, a standard deviation of about two point eight. | The noisy answer might be one hundred and twenty-one point three. Even an attacker who knows everyone else in the data can’t tell with confidence whether one particular patient is included. | Rounding the answer, or replacing a negative count with zero, is post-processing. It can’t weaken the guarantee, and it costs nothing. | But every release spends budget. If the same question could be asked again and again, the answers could be averaged to cancel out the noise, so a ledger tracks the total epsilon spent.

scenes.title: Repeated releases add up
scenes.yLabel: Total ε spent, by number of releases at ε = 0.1 each
scenes.say: Budgets add up. Under simple, sequential composition, a hundred releases at an epsilon of a tenth each cost ten, and a thousand releases cost a hundred, which is no meaningful protection at all. | Advanced composition gives a tighter bound. For many small releases, the total grows roughly with the square root of their number, at the cost of a tiny extra delta. A thousand releases cost about twenty-six instead of a hundred. | With a policy cap of ten, that means more than twice as many releases. Modern accountants, such as {Rényi~Renyi} differential privacy, are tighter still for the noisy steps of training. Whatever the method, the total must be tracked and capped.

scenes.title: DP-SGD: private training, one step at a time

nodes.label: Privacy accountant
nodes.sub: q, σ, steps and δ give ε

scenes.say: DP-SGD makes training itself differentially private. Each step starts with a batch, in which every record is included at random with a small probability, q. | The model computes a gradient for every example separately, rather than one gradient for the whole batch. That costs extra memory and time. | Each gradient is clipped, so its length is at most C. This caps how far any one record can move the model: its sensitivity. | Gaussian noise, with a standard deviation of sigma times C, is added to the sum of the clipped gradients, hiding any one record’s contribution. | The noisy average updates the weights, and the step repeats, often thousands of times. | A privacy accountant turns the sampling rate, the noise level, the number of steps and delta into the final epsilon. Without that calculation, a claim of differential privacy can’t be checked.

scenes.title: Reading a differential privacy claim
rows: Both values, for the whole release
A record, a user or a device?
Who sees raw data before noise?
An untrusted party holds raw data
scenes.say: Here is how to read a differential privacy claim. | First, ask for epsilon and delta, for the whole release. A claim with no numbers can’t be assessed. | Second, ask what one unit of privacy is: a record, a user or a device. If people contribute many records, record-level protection is much weaker for them. | Third, find out where the noise is added. In the central model, a curator sees raw data first; in the local model, noise is added on the device. | Fourth, ask which accountant was used, and whether hyperparameter tuning and repeated releases were counted. A budget that quietly restarts for each release isn’t a budget.

items: Epsilon bounds how much one person can change any outcome
Noise scales with sensitivity divided by epsilon
Budgets add up across releases; accountants track them
DP-SGD clips and adds noise at every training step
Ask for ε, δ, the unit of privacy and the accounting
scenes.say: To recap. | Epsilon bounds how much any one person’s data can change the probability of any outcome. | The noise needed scales with the sensitivity of the query divided by epsilon. | Budgets add up across releases, and accountants track the total. | DP-SGD clips each example’s gradient and adds noise at every training step. | And when anyone claims differential privacy, ask for epsilon, delta, the unit of privacy and the accounting.

blocks.md:
### The definition, precisely
A randomised mechanism is **(ε, δ)-differentially private** if, for any two datasets that differ in one person’s data, and any set of outcomes, the probability of the outcome with the person’s data is at most *e^ε* times the probability without it, plus δ.
- **ε (epsilon)** bounds the ratio. With ε = 1, no outcome becomes more than about 2.7 times more likely because of one person’s data; with ε = 10, the bound is about 22,000 times, a far weaker promise.
- **δ (delta)** is a small probability that the bound fails. It should be much smaller than one divided by the number of people in the data, for example 10⁻⁵ or less for 100,000 people. Pure ε-differential privacy has δ = 0.

### Mechanisms
- **Sensitivity (Δ)** is the most one person can change a query’s answer: 1 for a count, and for a sum, the cap applied to each person’s contribution.
- **Laplace mechanism:** adds noise with scale Δ ÷ ε and gives pure ε-differential privacy. For a count with ε = 0.5, the scale is 2 and the standard deviation about 2.8.
- **Gaussian mechanism:** adds normally distributed noise scaled to the L2 sensitivity. It gives (ε, δ)-differential privacy and composes well, which is why DP-SGD uses it.
- **Randomised response** and other **local** methods add noise on the user’s device, before collection.

### Composition and accounting
| Rule | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Sequential composition** | Releases from the same data add up: ε₁ + ε₂ + … |
| **Parallel composition** | Releases from separate groups of people cost only the largest ε |
| **Advanced composition** | Over many releases, the total grows roughly with the square root of their number, for a little extra δ |
| **Accountants** | Rényi DP, zero-concentrated DP and privacy loss distributions track noisy training tightly |
| **Post-processing** | Anything computed from a private output stays private, at no extra cost |

### DP-SGD in practice
DP-SGD (Abadi et al., 2016) changes every training step: sample a batch (each record with probability *q*), compute **per-example gradients**, **clip** each to a maximum length *C*, add **Gaussian noise** with standard deviation *σ × C* to the sum, then average and update. An **accountant** turns *q*, *σ*, the number of steps and δ into the final ε. **Opacus** (PyTorch), **TensorFlow Privacy** and **JAX Privacy** implement it; **OpenDP** and **Tumult Analytics** cover statistics. Expect lower accuracy, slower training and more memory. Larger datasets, and pre-training on public data before private fine-tuning, reduce the cost. Hyperparameter tuning on the private data also spends budget unless it is accounted for.

### Reading a claim
Ask for **ε and δ** for the whole release; the **unit of privacy** (a record, a user or a device; user-level protection covers everything a person contributed); the **central or local** model; the **accountant**, and whether tuning and repeated releases were counted; and **what is protected**, the model or only some outputs. Deployed values range from below 1 to well above 10: the 2020 US Census redistricting data used a total of ε = 19.61 (17.14 for persons and 2.47 for housing units). A large ε isn’t automatically unacceptable, but it needs justifying alongside other controls. NIST SP 800-226 (2025) offers a framework for evaluating these guarantees.

blocks.title: Reviewing a supplier’s differential privacy claim
items: Get the numbers
Ask for ε and δ for the whole release, not per query or per training epoch. A claim with no numbers can’t be assessed.
Find the unit
Check whether one record, one user or one device is protected. Where people contribute many records, record-level protection is weaker for them.
Locate the noise
Central differential privacy trusts a curator with raw data; local differential privacy adds noise on the device. Know who sees what before the noise.
Check the accounting
Ask which accountant was used, and whether hyperparameter tuning, retraining and repeated releases were counted.
Decide and record
Weigh ε against the sensitivity of the data and the other controls in place, then record the decision in the DPIA.

blocks.title: Apply the rules
pairs: One person can change a count by at most one
Two releases from the same data, ε 0.5 each
One release per region, ε 0.5 each, no overlap
Rounding a private result to whole numbers
Clip each example’s gradient, then add noise

blocks.title: Differential privacy calculations
blocks.md: Remember four rules: **smaller ε means more noise** and stronger privacy; the **noise scale is sensitivity ÷ ε**; budgets **add up** across releases from the same data but not across **separate groups** of people; and **post-processing is free**. A claim of differential privacy means little without ε, δ, the unit of privacy and the accounting.

q.q: A supplier says its fraud model was “trained with differential privacy, ε = 8”. Before relying on this in a DPIA, what should the privacy team establish FIRST?
o: Whether the training data was encrypted while the model was trained
The δ value, the unit of privacy and how the budget was accounted
Which noise distribution the supplier’s library uses by default
Whether the model’s accuracy matches a version trained without noise
q.why: An ε value alone can’t be interpreted: δ, what one unit of privacy is, and whether the accounting covered every step and release determine what the guarantee means. Encryption, the noise distribution and accuracy don’t change what the claim protects.

quiz.q: Under GDPR Article 25, what does data protection by default require?
o: Privacy-protective settings must be available for users who choose to switch them on
By default, only the personal data necessary for each specific purpose is processed
All personal data must be encrypted by default, wherever it is stored or sent
Default passwords on systems that process personal data must be changed before use
quiz.why: By default means protection applies without the person doing anything: only necessary data, limited access and limited retention. Optional privacy features and encryption alone don’t meet the requirement.

quiz.q: A retailer collected purchase data to fulfil orders. It now wants to train a model that infers customers’ health conditions from what they buy. Which principle is MOST directly at stake?
o: Storage limitation, because order data would be kept for longer than needed
Purpose limitation, because inferring health is a new and incompatible purpose
Accuracy, because some of the inferred conditions might turn out to be wrong
Integrity, because the model might be tampered with after it is deployed
quiz.why: Inferring health conditions is unrelated to fulfilling orders, and it creates special category data. It needs its own assessment and lawful basis; the other principles matter but are secondary.

quiz.q: Where consent is the lawful basis for training a model on personal data, which statement is correct?
o: Consent can be included in the general terms of service if they are clearly written
Consent must be specific, informed and unambiguous, and as easy to withdraw as to give
Consent stays valid indefinitely once given, even if the training purpose changes
Pre-ticked boxes are acceptable if the privacy notice explains the training use
quiz.why: GDPR consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, given by a clear affirmative act, and withdrawable at any time. Bundled terms, pre-ticked boxes and open-ended consent all fail.

quiz.q: Which statement about pseudonymised data under the GDPR is correct?
o: It is anonymous once direct identifiers are replaced, so the GDPR no longer applies
It remains personal data for a controller who holds the means to re-identify it
It may be published freely, provided the re-identification key is encrypted
It is a category defined only for health and genetic data used in clinical research
quiz.why: Pseudonymisation is a safeguard, not anonymisation. Whoever can re-identify the data, using a key or other information, is processing personal data.

quiz.q: In differential privacy, what does choosing a smaller epsilon (ε) do?
o: Adds less noise, giving more accurate results and weaker privacy
Adds more noise, giving stronger privacy and less accurate results
Removes noise entirely once enough records have been collected
Shrinks the dataset so that fewer records need to be protected
quiz.why: ε bounds how much any one person’s data can change the output. A smaller ε needs more noise, which strengthens privacy and reduces accuracy.

quiz.q: An organisation uses unsalted SHA-256 hashes of customers’ phone numbers as identifiers in a shared dataset. What is the MAIN weakness?
o: SHA-256 is too slow to compute for large datasets of phone numbers
Phone numbers are predictable, so hashing every possible number reverses them
Hashed values can’t be joined with other datasets for analysis
SHA-256 hashes are too long to store efficiently in most databases and analytics tools
quiz.why: The set of possible phone numbers is small enough to enumerate. Use a keyed hash (HMAC) or tokenisation, with the key held separately, and treat the result as pseudonymous personal data.

quiz.q: Which technique lets authorised payment systems recover card numbers while keeping them out of AI and analytics pipelines?
o: Generalising card numbers into ranges
Vaulted tokenisation of card numbers
Differential privacy on transactions
Suppressing the card number field
quiz.why: Tokenisation replaces card numbers with tokens downstream, while the vault lets a small set of authorised systems detokenise. Generalisation, noise and suppression can’t recover the original.

quiz.q: Under the GDPR, when must a controller normally notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach?
o: Within 24 hours of the breach occurring, in every case
Within 72 hours of becoming aware, unless unlikely to result in risk
Within 60 days of discovery, in line with the deadline for HIPAA breaches
Only once affected individuals have already been told
quiz.why: Article 33 requires notification without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to people.

quiz.q: Which statement about PCI DSS is correct?
o: It is a US federal law enforced by the Federal Trade Commission and state regulators
It is an industry standard enforced through card brands and acquirers
It applies only to banks that issue payment cards to consumers
It allows card security codes to be stored if they are encrypted
quiz.why: PCI DSS is a contractual industry standard. It applies to any entity that stores, processes or transmits card data, and it prohibits storing sensitive authentication data after authorisation, even encrypted.

quiz.q: Which HIPAA de-identification method relies on a qualified expert’s documented statistical analysis?
o: Safe Harbor
Expert Determination
Limited data set
Minimum necessary review
quiz.why: Expert Determination uses a qualified expert to conclude that re-identification risk is very small. Safe Harbor removes 18 identifier types instead.

quiz.q: A person’s data was used to fine-tune a large model, and they ask for erasure. Which option gives the HIGHEST assurance that the model no longer reflects their data?
o: Adding an output filter that blocks responses naming the person
Retraining the model on a dataset with their records fully removed
Applying an approximate unlearning method to the existing weights
Lowering the model’s temperature so it is less likely to regurgitate
quiz.why: A retrained model has never seen the data. Approximate unlearning is hard to verify, filters leave the data in the weights, and temperature changes remove nothing.

quiz.q: Which statement BEST describes a model’s prediction that an identifiable person has a particular health condition?
o: It isn’t personal data, because the person never provided it
It is personal data, and can be special category data too
It belongs to the model provider as intellectual property
It is anonymous, because it is only a statistical estimate
quiz.why: Inferences about identifiable people are personal data, and an inferred health condition is special category data, whether or not the inference is accurate.

quiz.q: A count is released with the Laplace mechanism at ε = 1. The analyst now wants to release it at ε = 0.25 instead. How does the noise change?
o: Its scale shrinks to a quarter of its size
Its scale grows fourfold, from 1 to 4
Its scale doubles, as it depends on √ε
It is unchanged; only δ is affected
quiz.why: The Laplace noise scale is sensitivity ÷ ε. For a count, the sensitivity is 1, so the scale rises from 1 to 4 as ε falls from 1 to 0.25: more noise, stronger privacy.

quiz.q: A health service releases one private statistic per region, each at ε = 0.5. Every patient belongs to exactly one region. What is the total privacy loss for any one patient?
o: ε = 0.5 multiplied by the number of regions
ε = 0.5, because the regions don’t overlap
ε = 1, the usual cap for any two releases
Unknown, since separate releases can’t be bounded
quiz.why: Under parallel composition, releases computed on disjoint groups of people cost only the largest ε, because each person’s data affects just one release.

quiz.q: What does the per-example gradient clipping step in DP-SGD achieve?
o: It removes duplicate records before each training step
It caps how much any single record can change each update
It encrypts the gradients so the server can’t read them
It stops the learning rate from becoming too large
quiz.why: Clipping bounds each example’s contribution, which sets the sensitivity that the Gaussian noise must hide. De-duplication, encryption and learning rate limits are separate matters.

quiz.q: A vendor’s differential privacy guarantee protects each record, but some customers contribute thousands of records each. What is the concern?
o: Those customers are protected more, since their records are averaged
Those customers are protected far less than the stated ε suggests
The guarantee is void unless every customer contributes one record
The guarantee applies, but only to the most recent record of each
quiz.why: Record-level protection weakens for people with many records, because their combined influence can be much larger than one record’s. User-level differential privacy protects everything a person contributes.

exam.q: A bank’s marketing team wants to reuse customer service chat transcripts, collected to resolve complaints, to fine-tune a model that writes personalised sales offers. The privacy notice mentions only complaint handling. What should the privacy lead recommend FIRST?
o: Proceed, since the bank already holds the transcripts lawfully and the fine-tuned model will stay in-house
Run a DPIA covering purpose compatibility and lawful basis, then update notices and offer opt-out or consent as needed
Strip names and account numbers from the transcripts and proceed, since de-identified free text falls entirely outside the GDPR
Ask the vendor to confirm in writing that the fine-tuning data won’t be used to improve its other models
exam.why: Marketing is a new purpose that needs a compatibility assessment and a lawful basis. Removing names doesn’t anonymise free-text transcripts, holding data lawfully for one purpose doesn’t cover another, and vendor terms address a different risk.

exam.q: A health research team plans to publish a dataset of patient visits with names removed but full postcodes, dates of birth and visit dates retained. What is the BEST assessment?
o: The dataset is anonymous, because names and record numbers have been removed and no direct identifiers remain
Postcodes, birth dates and visit dates allow linkage; generalise or suppress them and assess risk before release
The dataset can be published safely if downloaders must register and agree not to attempt re-identification
The dataset can be published once the file is encrypted and the key is sent only to approved researchers
exam.why: Combinations of quasi-identifiers single out most people. Generalisation, suppression or differential privacy, plus a re-identification risk assessment, are needed. Registration terms help but don’t anonymise, and encryption protects confidentiality, not identifiability.

exam.q: A company wants to publish weekly statistics on how staff use its internal AI assistant, broken down by department, without revealing any individual’s behaviour. Some departments have only three or four people. Which approach BEST meets the goal?
o: Publish exact counts for every department, since the statistics contain no names or employee identifiers
Apply differential privacy to the statistics, tracking the total privacy budget spent across weekly releases
Round every count to the nearest ten before publishing, which hides each individual’s behaviour each week
Share the department-level figures only with senior managers, who are trusted not to misuse them
exam.why: Small groups make exact or rounded counts revealing, and repeated releases compound the risk. Differential privacy gives a provable limit per release, and an accountant tracks the cumulative loss. Rounding offers no guarantee and can be undone by comparing releases.

exam.q: A European retailer uses an AI model to reject online credit applications automatically below a score threshold, with no human review. A rejected applicant asks why. Which response BEST meets GDPR requirements?
o: Decline to explain, because the scoring model is a trade secret that the retailer is entitled to protect in full
Explain the main factors and logic involved, and offer human review and a clear way to contest the decision
Confirm the decision was made by a validated algorithm, which on its own meets the GDPR’s transparency duty
Offer a manual reapplication route instead, since Article 22 only applies to decisions made by public bodies
exam.why: A solely automated credit refusal falls under Article 22. The applicant is entitled to meaningful information about the logic involved, and to safeguards including human intervention and the right to contest. Trade secrets can’t justify a blanket refusal.

exam.q: A retailer’s new voice assistant takes phone orders and records every call for model improvement. Customers read out their card number and security code during the call. What is the MOST important change?
o: Encrypt the call recordings with strong keys, which makes it acceptable to retain the security codes they contain
Keep card data out of recordings with keypad entry or pause-and-resume, and purge any stored security codes
Restrict access to the recordings to the data science team that uses them for model training and evaluation
Keep the recordings for no more than 12 months before deletion, in line with the retailer’s retention schedule
exam.why: PCI DSS prohibits storing sensitive authentication data after authorisation, even when encrypted. The fix is to stop capturing it and remove what has been stored; access limits and retention schedules don’t make the storage permissible.

exam.q: A lender’s data scientists want to check whether their credit model treats ethnic groups differently, but the training data contains no ethnicity information. The DPO is concerned about minimisation. What is the BEST approach?
o: Abandon fairness testing, because collecting ethnicity data for any purpose would breach the minimisation principle
Use ethnicity data for testing only where strictly necessary, under a legal basis, segregated, then delete it
Add ethnicity as a permanent model input, so that the model can learn to correct for any bias automatically
Infer each applicant’s ethnicity from their name and postcode, and keep it on file for future credit decisions
exam.why: Bias can’t be measured without group information, but sensitive data should be used only where strictly necessary, with a legal basis and safeguards, and deleted afterwards. The EU AI Act provides for this. Using ethnicity in decisions, or keeping inferred ethnicity, creates new risks.

exam.q: An AI assistant repeatedly tells users that a named private individual has a criminal conviction. This is false, and the individual complains. What should the provider do FIRST?
o: Explain that outputs are probabilistic predictions, so the GDPR’s accuracy principle doesn’t apply to model outputs
Suppress false outputs about them now, fix any grounding sources, investigate, and answer the rectification request
Begin a full retraining of the model, and reply to the complaint only once the new version is deployed
Ask the individual to provide proof of a clean criminal record before considering any change to outputs
exam.why: False personal data in outputs engages the accuracy principle and the right to rectification. Immediate suppression limits ongoing harm while the cause is fixed; waiting for retraining or demanding proof leaves the harm in place.

exam.q: A product team plans to let analysts run unlimited differentially private queries against an HR dataset, each at ε = 0.1, with no record kept of how many have been run. What is the MOST significant problem?
o: An ε of 0.1 adds too little noise to protect anyone in the dataset
Repeated queries add up, so the overall privacy loss has no upper bound
Analysts could see the noise values and subtract them from results
Each query must use a different noise mechanism to remain private
exam.why: Privacy loss composes: with unlimited queries the total ε grows without limit, and averaging repeated answers can cancel the noise. A privacy accountant must track and cap the budget.

exam.q: A data scientist tuned DP-SGD hyperparameters by training 40 models on the private dataset, then reported the ε of the final run only. What should the privacy reviewer conclude?
o: The ε is accurate, since only the final model will ever be deployed
The ε is understated, as tuning on the private data also spends budget
The ε is overstated, since the earlier runs were all discarded
The ε is irrelevant, as DP-SGD protects privacy regardless of settings
exam.why: Every training run on the private data leaks information, including through the choice of the best run. Tuning must be included in the accounting, or done on public or separate data.

exam.q: A team releases a differentially private model. It then publishes an adjusted version, derived only from the private model’s weights and public data, with no further access to the training data. What happens to the privacy budget?
o: The budget doubles, since a second model has now been released
No extra budget is spent, as post-processing can’t weaken the guarantee
The guarantee is lost, since the model was modified after training
The new version needs a fresh budget, set by the team that adjusted it
exam.why: Anything computed from a differentially private output without touching the private data again is post-processing, so it keeps the original guarantee at no extra cost.
